Server Administration Guide, "Managing organizations": "In the Organizations section, you can manage all the organizations in your realm. Creating an organization: Click Create Organization. An organization has the following settings: Name — a user-friendly name for the organization. The name is unique within a realm."

Server Administration Guide documents "W3C Web Authentication (WebAuthn)" setup ("Enable WebAuthn authentication in the default browser flow", "WebAuthn together with Two-Factor", "LoginLess WebAuthn") and a dedicated "Passkeys" section: "Passkey Authentication with Conditional UI or autofill", "Passkeys Authentication with Modal UI", "Passkey Mediation".

Server Administration Guide, "Managing users and groups through SCIM": built-in SCIM endpoints per realm ("Enabling SCIM for a realm", "Obtaining the SCIM API base URL", "Setting up a service account client"), with protected admin users excluded: "resources can only be managed through the Admin Console or the Admin REST API, never through SCIM."

Server Administration Guide, "Device authorization grant": "This is used by clients running on internet-connected devices that have limited input capabilities or lack a suitable browser." The OIDC layers reference documents the endpoint: "/realms/{realm-name}/protocol/openid-connect/auth/device ... used to obtain a device code and a user code."

OIDC layers reference, "Client credentials": "Client Credentials are used when clients (applications and services) want to obtain access on behalf of themselves rather than on behalf of a user." Clients authenticate via client_id/client_secret or JWT, backing service accounts for machine-to-machine access.

Server Administration Guide documents the Admin CLI: Keycloak "packages the Admin CLI server distribution with the execution scripts in the bin directory. The Linux script is called kcadm.sh", enabling scripted administration of realms, users, roles, and clients; the same operations are available over the Admin REST API.

Server Administration Guide, brute force protection events: "User disabled by permanent lockout — Brute force protection disabled the user account permanently due to too many login failures. User disabled by temporary lockout — Brute force protection disabled the user account temporarily due to too many login failures."

Keycloak site, Identity Brokering and Social Login: "Enabling login with social networks is easy to add through the admin console. It's just a matter of selecting the social network you want to add. No code or changes to your application" — brokering also covers external OpenID Connect or SAML identity providers.

Keycloak site, User Federation: "Keycloak has built-in support to connect to existing LDAP or Active Directory servers. You can also implement your own provider if you have users in other stores, such as a relational database."

Authorization Services guide: fine-grained, resource-level authorization — "A resource is part of the assets of an application and the organization... In authorization policy terminology, a resource is the object being protected", with policies evaluated via UMA permission tickets and client-credentials-obtained PATs.

One team has used Keycloak for 6-7 years. It has run very stable in clustered mode, with many external IdPs integrated for SSO across several software stacks. A Java background helped them not worry about its memory use.

Keycloak is best treated as a "pet": it takes a while to warm up. It is powerful and configurable, but plays poorly with infrastructure-as-code. A realm can be loaded from JSON, but keeping changes synced afterward is hard.

A startup tried Keycloak and found it needed a lot of memory, was very slow to start, and had huge Docker images. Community support felt less active than other FOSS projects, so they ditched it for a proprietary solution.
Uses Keycloak for all authentication, in the cloud on Linux and in Windows enterprise environments, with SSO for Node-RED, Grafana, ASP.NET and VueJS apps. "Was fairly easy to move from Auth0."
Biggest complaint is poor documentation: you need various flags for your use case, which means lots of googling and Stack Overflow. Options changed in 17.x, so many guides are outdated.
Configuration was painful on the Wildfly/JBoss version, but on Quarkus it is "mostly trivial now." The only non-environment-variable settings needed in production were for Infinispan discovery.
One user dropped Keycloak because its roughly 2 GiB of RAM was too much for SSO on a tiny VPS, and switched to static htpasswd.

Nothing made sense until learning OAuth2/OIDC. The docs can't be searched; admin UI tooltips helped more. "It never failed for me. Even upgrading from 7.x.x to 16.x.x somehow just worked." The Docker image is still big (562MB).

Keycloak works great but is hard to understand without OAuth/OIDC knowledge, and it is heavyweight. Running it means learning Wildfly quirks, Infinispan, Java and Docker. Unless you already deploy Java apps, it is a serious administrative burden.
Keycloak doesn't make it easy to stop users changing their own email. Where service providers use email as the username, that makes impersonation trivial.
Keycloak is great for authenticating against on-prem AD. It isolates messy OU and domain layouts and exposes a simple OAuth 2.0/OIDC interface.
"I've run keycloak securing internet facing apps with ~1000 users for years. It's so stable, I usually forget it's even there."

Automating resources with Ansible is hard because the Keycloak API is inconsistent. Some GET methods return incomplete payloads, and some endpoints don't save on POST but do on update, which makes idempotency very hard.
After Okta told them, as paying customers, to pay extra or leave, one team switched to Keycloak and "never looked back. It's stable, customizable, well engineered and relatively easy to work with."
Keycloak feels like clunky 90s enterprise software. Running it on OpenShift was hell: not made for containers, clustering basically impossible, and it needed obscure startup scripts patched.

One team used Keycloak for SSO across 10+ Java services. Setting it up with LDAP was easy, Google SSO took a few settings, and it ran on Docker without problems. The UI was at times clunky but the docs were good. "I would recommend it to anyone."

Biggest problem is that config is stored in the database, so there's no supported way to test changes and promote them to production; you click around the UI. The third-party keycloak-config-cli helps but isn't as good as first-party gitops config.

Keycloak has no support for opaque tokens. On the front end, expired login-page tokens cause errors instead of an automatic retry, and multiple tabs can show "already logged in" errors and lose the redirect URL.

Commenters discussed CVE-2023-6927, which bypasses redirect URI validation for clients whose redirect URI ends in * (Keycloak < 23.0.4). One noted that Keycloak's default admin and account clients use wildcards; another argued that wildcard redirects in production are the operator's fault.

Running Keycloak as an enterprise Java app on Wildfly means frequent high/critical CVEs in bundled components like SnakeYAML, Apache SSHD, H2 and Infinispan. You probably don't use them but must patch them anyway.
